Dominance effect sizes for ordinal variables

d_ord.Rd

Calculate dominance-based effect sizes for ordinal variables.

Usage

d_ord(x, meta = NULL)

Arguments

x

data. See details.

meta

either NULL or a named list.

Value

Estimates with verbose explanations.

Details

Calculate the following:

  • stochastic difference (aka Glass rank-biserial correlation);

  • adjusted stochastic difference (aka Goodman and Kruskal's gamma);

  • dominance (aka common language effect size);

  • measure of stochastic superiority (aka Vargha and Delaney's A);

  • adjusted dominance; and

  • generalized odds ratio; and

  • win odds.

x can contain either known parameter values or observed counts.

x should be a data.frame with 2 rows. It can optionally contain a variable called group, indicating the name of the group. In addition, it must contain one variable for each possible outcome (2 or more outcomes). The outcome variables must be ordered from best to worst.

The outcome variables can contain one of the following:

  • event probabilities, which are known parameters, and which must be between 0 and 1 and add up to 1; or

  • the number of events.

In the special case when there are exactly two outcome variables and they are called k and n, this is taken to be binary data: k is the number of events; n is the sample size – it is the number of events plus the number of non-events.

Optionally, x can have an attribute called "meta", which must be a named list.

See also

Other es: d_bin(), d_cont(), d_np(), d_one(), d_pair()

Examples

# Number of events for each outcome
d_ord(comparison_data$TB)

#> │ Equivalence dependence │ Equivalence dependent. This effect size's possible range narrows toward │
#> │                        │ the point of probabilistic equality (no effect) as the probability of a │
#> │                        │ tied outcome grows, so it correctly reports a small effect when most    │

#> │                        │ .001                                                                    │

#> │ Meaning                │ The correlation between group (Streptomycin vs. Bed rest) and outcome   │
#> │                        │ is 0.58, if we ignore all pairs with the same outcome.                  │

#> │                        │ portray a relationship as large even when ties are common.              │

#> ┌────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
#> │ What                   │ Value                                                                   │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Effect size            │ Adjusted stochastic difference (ASD)                                    │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Result                 │ ASD (X1 vs. X2) = 0.26                                                  │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Meaning                │ The correlation between group (X1 vs. X2) and outcome is 0.26, if we    │
#> │                        │ ignore all pairs with the same outcome.                                 │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Equivalence dependence │ Not equivalence dependent. This effect size's range does not depend on  │
#> │                        │ the probability of a tie, because tied pairs are divided out and only   │
#> │                        │ the pairs that are distinguishable are measured. It can therefore       │
#> │                        │ portray a relationship as large even when ties are common.              │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Other names            │ Goodman and Kruskal's gamma. For binary variables, ASD = Yule's Q, also │
#> │                        │ known as Yule coefficient of association.                               │
#> └────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
#> 
#>                                        Results: Dominance (D)                                       
#> ┌────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
#> │ What                   │ Value                                                                   │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Effect size            │ Dominance (D)                                                           │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Result                 │ D (X1 vs. X2) = 41.7%                                                   │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Meaning                │ The probability of a better [variable] for X1 vs. X2 is 41.7%.          │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Equivalence dependence │ Equivalence dependent. This effect size's possible range narrows toward │
#> │                        │ the point of probabilistic equality (no effect) as the probability of a │
#> │                        │ tied outcome grows, so it correctly reports a small effect when most    │
#> │                        │ pairs would have the same outcome regardless of the group. This is a    │
#> │                        │ desirable property in many settings, including the treatment and        │
#> │                        │ control group setting, since ties are part of the answer, not a         │
#> │                        │ nuisance to be divided out.                                             │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Other names            │ Common language effect size (CLES); Grissom and Kim's probability of    │
#> │                        │ superiority; stress-strength model; and reliability.                    │
#> └────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
#> 
#>                           Results: Measure of stochastic superiority (MSS)                          
#> ┌────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
#> │ What                   │ Value                                                                   │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Effect size            │ Measure of stochastic superiority (MSS)                                 │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Result                 │ MSS (X1 vs. X2) = 58.5%                                                 │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Meaning                │ The probability of a better latent variable for [variable] for X1 vs.   │
#> │                        │ X2 is 58.5%.                                                            │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Equivalence dependence │ Equivalence dependent. This effect size's possible range narrows toward │
#> │                        │ the point of probabilistic equality (no effect) as the probability of a │
#> │                        │ tied outcome grows, so it correctly reports a small effect when most    │
#> │                        │ pairs would have the same outcome regardless of the group. This is a    │
#> │                        │ desirable property in many settings, including the treatment and        │
#> │                        │ control group setting, since ties are part of the answer, not a         │
#> │                        │ nuisance to be divided out.                                             │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Other names            │ Vargha and Delaney's A; nonoverlap of all pairs; probabilistic index;   │
#> │                        │ probability of a superior outcome; concordance index c; proportion of   │
#> │                        │ similar responses; relative effect. Closely related to the area under a │
#> │                        │ receiver operating characteristic curve.                                │
#> └────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
#> 
#>                                   Results: Adjusted dominance (AD)                                  
#> ┌────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
#> │ What                   │ Value                                                                   │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Effect size            │ Adjusted dominance (AD)                                                 │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Result                 │ AD (X1 vs. X2) = 62.8%                                                  │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Meaning                │ The probability of a better [variable] for X1 vs. X2 is 62.8%, if we    │
#> │                        │ ignore all pairs with the same outcome. Alternatively, the probability  │
#> │                        │ of a better latent variable for [variable] for X1 vs. X2 is 62.8% (but  │
#> │                        │ using different assumptions than for MSS).                              │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Equivalence dependence │ Not equivalence dependent. This effect size's range does not depend on  │
#> │                        │ the probability of a tie, because tied pairs are divided out and only   │
#> │                        │ the pairs that are distinguishable are measured. It can therefore       │
#> │                        │ portray a relationship as large even when ties are common.              │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Other names            │ -                                                                       │
#> └────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

#>                                Results: Generalized odds ratio (GOR)                                
#> ┌────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
#> │ What                   │ Value                                                                   │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Effect size            │ Generalized odds ratio (GOR)                                            │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Result                 │ GOR (X1 vs. X2) = 1.7                                                   │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Meaning                │ The ratio of the probability of a better [variable] for X1 to the       │
#> │                        │ probability of a better [variable] for X2 is 1.7.                       │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Equivalence dependence │ Not equivalence dependent. This effect size's range does not depend on  │
#> │                        │ the probability of a tie, because tied pairs are divided out and only   │
#> │                        │ the pairs that are distinguishable are measured. It can therefore       │
#> │                        │ portray a relationship as large even when ties are common.              │
#> ├────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
#> │ Other names            │ Agresti's generalized odds ratio for stochastic dominance; win ratio.   │
#> │                        │ For binary variables, GOR = odds ratio (OR). For continuous variables,  │
#> │                        │ GOR = odds.                                                             │
#> └────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

#> │                        │ pairs would have the same outcome regardless of the group. This is a    │
#> │                        │ desirable property in many settings, including the treatment and        │
#> │                        │ control group setting, since ties are part of the answer, not a         │
#> │                        │ nuisance to be divided out.                                             │
